extracted.intended_audience: naturalists and educated general readers interested in evolutionary theory (Darwin's contemporaries and later readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the conditions, mechanisms, and circumstantial factors that favour or impede natural selection and sexual selection across plants and animals, with examples and reasoning. Useful as a checklist of biological principles that must hold or be considered when arguing that natural selection can produce adaptations or new species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual selection (male competition and female choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: When males and females differ, differences have often been mainly caused by sexual selection; individual males have had slight advantages over other males in weapons, means of defence, or charms and transmitted these to male offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: male salmons fighting, stag-beetles with huge mandibles, mane of the lion, shoulder-pad of the boar, hooked jaw of the male salmon. Among birds: rivalry by singing, display of plumage (rock-thrush, birds of Paradise), and female choice producing marked effects over many generations. Note: not all male-peculiar traits are clearly useful or attractive (some may be inexplicable or 'monstrosities').

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural selection acts by preservation and accumulation of small inherited modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural selection can act only by the preservation and accumulation of infinitesimally small inherited modifications, each profitable to the preserved being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to geology: slow, repeated small causes (like coast-waves) can produce great results. Natural selection therefore implies extremely slow change rather than sudden creation or great, sudden modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection favours traits increasing survival in current ecological context
rubrics_metrics.description: Traits that improve an individual's chance of surviving under current conditions (strength, fleetness, craftiness, etc.) will be preserved and passed on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: if deer (fast prey) increase, swift wolves will be favoured. Comparison to artificial selection: man can improve fleetness of greyhounds by selection; analogous unconscious selection occurs in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heritable behavioural tendencies can be selected
rubrics_metrics.description: Innate tendencies to pursue certain prey or show certain behaviours can be inherited and thus be acted on by natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domestic examples: different cats inherit tendencies to hunt rats vs mice vs birds. If such habits benefit survival, they may lead to new varieties over generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection for floral traits promoting pollinator visitation and cross-pollination
rubrics_metrics.description: Plants that produce nectaries or floral structures that attract insects (nectar, larger glands, placement of stamens/pistils) will be visited more and thus be more frequently crossed, gaining advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nectar-excreting glands, larger anthers producing more pollen despite pollen loss to pollen-collecting insects. Placement of reproductive organs relative to pollinator size and habits matters. Case: holly male and female trees and bee-mediated pollination over distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological division of labour (separation of sexes) can be advantageous
rubrics_metrics.description: When regular cross-pollination by insects occurs, producing staminate flowers on some individuals and pistillate on others (or separation within flowers) may be advantageous and thus selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: holly trees bearing only male or only female flowers, with corresponding reduction of pistil or anther function. Slight tendencies toward impotence of one sex in culture may be exaggerated by natural selection under cross-pollination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal adaptation (coevolution) between plants and pollinators
rubrics_metrics.description: Slight beneficial deviations in floral form and in insect morphology (e.g., proboscis length/shape) may be mutually selected, producing highly coadapted relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: hive-bee can suck nectar from Trifolium incarnatum but not from Trifolium pratense; corolla tube length selects for appropriate pollinator morphology. Mutual modification can occur simultaneously or sequentially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage of cross-fertilisation (outcrossing) over self-fertilisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Crosses between different varieties or strains produce vigour and fertility; close inbreeding/self-fertilisation diminishes vigour and fertility. This suggests that occasional crossing with another individual is generally advantageous or indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: breeders' experience, exposed reproductive organs in many flowers, papilionaceous flower dependence on bee visits, experimental reductions in fertility when visits prevented. Implication: floral forms that facilitate cross-pollination are favoured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Floral contrivances that prevent selfing imply selection for outcrossing
rubrics_metrics.description: Many flowers show mechanisms (timing of anther/stigma maturity, physical arrangements) that prevent self-fertilisation, indicating selection for cross-fertilisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Lobelia fulgens where pollen is swept out before stigma is receptive; anthers bursting before stigma is ready or stigma ready before pollen, effectively separating sexes temporally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pollen prepotency phenomena (relative success of different pollen sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: When pollen from different sources is present, pollen of a plant's own species (or sometimes own variety) may have a prepotent effect, influencing which pollen successfully fertilises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations: in some cases, a plant's own pollen destroys influence of foreign species' pollen (reducing hybridisation), while in cases of distinct varieties pollen of a distinct variety may be prepotent and produce mongrelized seedlings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex separation in trees aids cross-pollination between individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Where many flowers occur on a single tree, separation of sexes (or unisexual flowers) increases the chance that pollen is carried from tree to tree rather than only within the same tree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin's tabulations: trees of many Orders more often have separated sexes than other plants (with some regional exceptions). This tendency mitigates the problem of many flowers on one individual acting as a single reproductive unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairing and the necessity of occasional cross in animals
rubrics_metrics.description: Most vertebrates, insects, and many other large groups pair for each birth; hermaphrodites often also pair—suggesting that two individuals usually concur in reproduction rather than perpetual self-fertilisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terrestrial animals: Darwin found no clear case of self-fertilising terrestrial animals. Aquatic animals can have occasional cross via water currents. Cirripedes were once a difficulty but shown to sometimes cross.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intercrossing maintains vigour and uniformity within species/varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasional intercrosses keep individuals of the same species or variety true and uniform and counteract the degeneration associated with prolonged self-fertilisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intercrossing especially affects animals that unite for each birth and those that wander and breed slowly. Even rare intercrosses can produce offspring with much greater vigour and fertility than long selfed lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of variability and population size favour selection
rubrics_metrics.description: A large amount of inheritable and diversified variability is favourable, but even mere individual differences suffice. A large number of individuals increases the chance of profitable variations appearing in any given period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large populations compensate for lesser per-individual variability by producing more variants overall; breeders prefer seed from large bodies to reduce chances of cross with other varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intercrossing and gene flow can retard divergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Free intercrossing (gene flow) across an area tends to retard the divergence promoted by local natural selection, especially in continuous, large areas where conditions grade into one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intercrossing most affects animals that unite for each birth, wander, and breed slowly (e.g., birds), leading to varieties being generally confined to separated countries rather than continuous areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation promotes formation of new varieties/species
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolation (geographic, ecological, or other) prevents immigration and intercrossing, allows time for local varieties to be perfected by selection, and thus favours the production of new species, particularly on islands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Islands often have high proportions of endemic species. Isolation acts both by checking immigration of better-adapted competitors and by preventing gene flow that would swamp new varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large continental areas often more favourable for long-lasting, widely-spreading species
rubrics_metrics.description: Although small isolated areas may produce new forms, large continuous areas favour production of many new forms that endure and spread, because they support more individuals, more complex interactions, and stronger competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large areas provide diverse conditions and competitors; improved forms from large areas are more likely to be victorious and give rise to further diversification. Oscillations of level creating broken conditions can combine benefits of isolation and largeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecological and behavioural separation aid local divergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Varieties can remain distinct within the same area when they haunt different stations, breed at different seasons, or prefer to pair assortatively; such separations allow local divergence despite potential intercrossing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes examples and claims these mechanisms can allow distinct varieties to persist in the same general area for long periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rate and intermittency of selection: long timescales and slowness
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural selection generally acts very slowly, often only at long intervals, and usually on only a few inhabitants of the same region at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Action depends on places in the 'polity of nature' being available, occurrence of favourable variations, occasional physical changes, and on the retardant effect of intercrossing. Slow action accords with geological evidence of gradual change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of favourable variations and limits to selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can be effected by natural selection unless favourable variations occur; variation itself is apparently always a very slow process, and absence of favourable variants limits selection's power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection's power is also limited by intercrossing, population size, time available, and competition. Even so, prolonged artificial selection by humans shows what may be possible given sustained selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extinction linked to natural selection through preservation of advantageous variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural selection acts solely through the preservation of variations advantageous in some way, which consequently endure; extinction is intimately connected with this process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin signals that extinction will be discussed more fully in Geology chapter; here he notes that selection's preference for certain variants affects which forms persist and which go extinct.
